short: A positive share of large prime gaps

title.title: A positive proportion of large prime gaps
title.subtitle: Claim: for every $C > 0$, a positive proportion of gaps $p_{n+1} - p_n$ exceed $C \log p_n$

object.caption: $p_{n+1} - p_n$ for the first primes; marked: gaps larger than $\log p_n$ (the case $C = 1$)

beats.text: Gaps between consecutive primes: near $p$ the average gap is about $\log p$
Marked: gaps above $\log p_n$. Does a fixed share exceed $C \log p_n$ for every $C$?
The claim: yes, for every $C$, though the share $c(C)$ is tiny

achievement.label: Large prime gaps for every C, and the p_n/n question
statement: \#\{n \le N : p_{n+1} - p_n > C \log p_n\} \ge c(C)\, N
achievement.context: Before: gaps beyond any multiple of $\log p_n$ occur (Westzynthius 1931), but not a positive share
achievement.note: The constants $c(C)$ are not explicit, and certainly tiny for large $C$

verify.detail: In Lean: the corollary on $p_n/n$, not the full gap theorem
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean docs and allowed axioms; we did not build it

sources.quote: For every fixed C > 0 there is c(C) > 0 with #{n <= N : p_{n+1} - p_n > C log p_n} >= c(C) N for all large N.
Positive proportion of gaps larger than C times average for every C was open
19 pages, constants c(C) not explicit and certainly tiny for large C.
the Lean doc presents it as a supplement rather than the full gap theorem

plain: Gaps between primes average about $\log p$; this shows a fixed share of gaps are many times longer

steps: Weight each stretch of numbers with a sieve
Under the weights, a prime likely starts the stretch
and the next $C \log X$ numbers are likely all composite
So a positive share of gaps are long
